title: What Are We Actually Creating?
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer opens with the observation that busyness and activity can crowd out the most important leadership question: not what did we mean, and not how hard did we work, but what is actually happening because of how we are leading? The piece argues that the industrial logic of constant production — optimized for output, speed, and scale — has migrated from factories into how people organize their work lives, their educational institutions, and their sense of self, with the result that activity has become a substitute for discernment. Schafer introduces the 'Real World Results' component of her Leadership Connection Model: an invitation to look beyond intention and activity to what is genuinely being created. The article's most practical move is its definition of citizen leadership: not only asking 'What can I do?' but also asking 'What is my doing creating?' The first question can lead to motion; the second leads to discernment. Schafer argues that discernment — the willingness to slow down, notice what the current trajectory is producing, and be honest about the gap between activity and outcome — may be the leadership capacity most urgently needed in the present moment.
points: The organizing question of the article is a shift from activity to outcome: not what did we intend, not how hard did we work, not how much did we care — but what is actually being created by how we are living and leading?

Industrial logic has colonized every domain of modern life, measuring worth by output, speed, and scale. The result is organizations and individuals that confuse responsiveness with contribution, productivity with purpose, and exhaustion with importance.

Citizen Leadership adds a second question to the standard leadership question. 'What can I do?' leads to motion; 'What is my doing creating?' leads to discernment. Discernment — not more doing — is what allows a leader to notice when the current path is not producing the life or the impact they seek.

The gap between activity and outcome can be vast even when the activity is genuinely good work. Years of good-faith effort inside systems, organizations, and communities may not be producing trust, dignity, vitality, or shared capacity if the larger conditions are not improving.

Discernment requires a specific willingness: to stop, feel the consequences of current choices, and ask whether the pace of activity is in service to life or has become a way to avoid noticing what is not working. The answer is not always to do more.
quotes: Sometimes we are so busy doing good things that we forget to ask what our actions are actually creating. We attend the meeting, send the email, make the plan, launch the program. We respond to the request, add the appointment, finish the task, take the call, move the project forward.
Activity is not the same as impact. Movement is not always progress. And being busy, even with worthy things, does not necessarily mean we are creating the results we most deeply desire.

We can confuse responsiveness with contribution, productivity with purpose, full calendars with meaningful engagement, exhaustion with importance. We can confuse keeping up with being alive and then wonder why the results do not match the effort.

Real World Results, in the Leadership Connection Model, asks us to look beyond intention and activity to what is actually being created. Not what did we mean? Not how hard did we work? Not how much did we care? Those questions matter, but they are incomplete.
A Citizen Leader does not only ask, What can I do? A Citizen Leader also asks, What is my doing creating? The first question can lead to motion. The second leads to discernment.

Discernment helps us step back from the momentum of the familiar and notice whether continuing on the same trajectory is actually taking us where we want to go. It asks us to tell the truth about systems that are active but not effective.
